einzeiler: A literary walking tour through the secret history and hidden streets of Edinburgh.
kurzfassung: This episode explores the literary and cultural history of Edinburgh through a walking tour of its iconic locations. The hosts discuss works by Muriel Spark, Kate Atkinson, Robert Burns, and James Hogg while navigating the city's unique mix of gothic superstition and enlightenment rationalism. Stops along the way include the old town, the Edinburgh Festival, and the famous Oxford Bar featured in Ian Rankin's Rebus novels.
stichpunkte: Walking through Marchmont, the inspiration for settings in Muriel Spark's The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
Examining the chaos and crowds of the Edinburgh Festival through Kate Atkinson's novel One Good Turn
Reading 16th and 18th-century poems by William Dunbar and Robert Ferguson detailing the city's historical squalor
Exploring the religious struggles of the Reformation and Mary, Queen of Scots
Discussing King James VI's treatise on witchcraft, Demonology, and its connection to Macbeth
Analyzing James Hogg's 1824 novel The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner
Exploring the Scottish Enlightenment and David Hume's radical philosophy
Ending the tour at the Oxford Bar, a recurring location in Ian Rankin's Inspector Rebus novels

clips.hook: Why Edinburgh's orderliness makes rebellion stand out
clips.text: The hosts note that the calm and structured atmosphere of traditional tenement neighborhoods makes rebellious behavior much more disruptive.

clips.hook: Northern Gothic architecture versus southern romance
clips.text: The city is described as featuring an austere northern sandstone aesthetic rather than the lush gothic styles found in warmer European regions.

clips.hook: Superstition and reason existing side by side
clips.text: The hosts reflect on how Edinburgh perpetually balances scientific progress with an inescapable undercurrent of spectral folklore.
David Hume's radical idea that human minds are merely bundles of sensory impressions is linked directly to modern skepticism surrounding artificial intelligence.

clips.hook: A city that constantly feeds on its own past
clips.text: Quoting Ian Rankin, the hosts describe Edinburgh as a place obsessed with its own history, comparing it to a serpent biting its own tail.

beschreibung:
SLOB is in Edinburgh for the International Book Festival. Join us on a walking tour of literary Edinburgh. From Mary Queen of Scots and James VI of Scotland, obsessed with witch hunts and an early anti-tobacco campaigner, to Muriel Spark and slum tourism in The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie. We walk from the gentrified streets of Marchmont and Bruntsfield, across the Meadows, and into the rough and tumble of the Old Town, a maze of cobbled streets and old buildings crowded on the hillside below the Edinburgh Castle. Cameos from Ian Rankin and Kate Atkinson, William Shakespeare, Samuel Johnson and James Boswell, and of course, Sir Walter Scott. Come through Edinburgh with SLOB and relish its very pungent history in a world before modern sanitation.

Mr. Johnson and I walked arm-in-arm up the High-street, to my house in James’s court: it was a dusky night: I could not prevent his being assailed by the evening effluvia of Edinburgh. … As we marched slowly along, he grumbled in my ear, ‘I smell you in the dark!’ But he acknowledged that the breadth of the street, and the loftiness of the buildings on each side, made a noble appearance.
